questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Life of Early Humans: Hunting-Gathering' refers to.
questions.a: Before civilisation, humans lived as hunting-gathering bands, moving with seasons and animals, using stone tools and fire, and leaving their story in rock paintings and tool sites that archaeologists excavate.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Life of Early Humans: Hunting-Gathering'.
questions.a: Move, hunt, gather, adapt: early life followed the rhythm of nature.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Agricultural Revolution' refers to.
questions.a: Learning to grow crops and tame animals transformed human life: farming fixed people to fields, surplus food supported larger settlements, and villages grew where hunting bands had wandered - the first step towards civilisation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Agricultural Revolution'.
questions.a: Seeds changed history: agriculture rooted people and produced surplus.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Agricultural Revolution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 4 (source: iest104.txt sections on the beginning of farming)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Beginning of Civilisation' refers to.
questions.a: Civilisation flowered where surplus, cities and organisation met: river valleys supported writing, monumental building, craft specialisation, trade and organised states - marking a decisive new stage in the human story.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Beginning of Civilisation'.
questions.a: Surplus built cities, cities demanded writing and states: civilisation's toolkit.
